claims.text: Introducing an intermediate moderate-temperature dwell during rapid heating and cooling changes the balance between precursor decomposition and atomic diffusion.
The intermediate dwell produces asynchronous nucleation.
Asynchronous nucleation promotes localized elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation.
Rapid thermal processing of these precursors uses peak temperatures above approximately 1100 K and cooling rates of approximately 10^4–10^5 K/s.
The individual metal precursors can have substantially different decomposition or reduction kinetics.
Dwell duration modulates transient atomic diffusion lengths.
Dwell duration modulates nucleation kinetics and the spatial overlap of precursor decomposition events.
Atomic mobility is limited when mixed solid precursors are reduced under kinetically constrained conditions.
Under standard rapid synthesis, limited atomic mobility forces nearly simultaneous precursor reduction.
Nearly simultaneous precursor reduction favors homogeneous single-phase formation.
Adding a dwell modestly increases atomic mobility.
Different precursor decomposition kinetics become asynchronous during the dwell and generate separate nucleation events.
A dwell-treated sample will exhibit more elemental segregation or secondary phases than a zero-dwell sample.
Segregation or secondary phases will be observable through heterogeneous morphology, elemental-mapping discrepancies, or distinct diffraction peaks.
Rapid heating and cooling without an intermediate dwell can produce a homogeneously mixed single-phase HEA nanoparticle baseline.
The proposed dwell effect is expected primarily when precursor decomposition temperatures differ significantly and diffusion is limited.
An excessively long or poorly chosen dwell can cause nanoparticle coalescence or agglomeration.
An excessively long or poorly chosen dwell can instead cause complete homogenization.
The optimal dwell time, temperature window, and diffusion threshold are not known.
Failure of all tested dwell conditions to produce statistically significant segregation or secondary phases relative to a zero-dwell control would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that poorly selected or excessively long dwells may yield complete homogenization, whereas the falsification rule treats failure of the tested dwell periods to induce segregation as decisive. Unless the experiment demonstrably spans the unknown effective dwell window, homogeneous results could reflect out-of-bound conditions rather than falsify the mechanism.
